nodes.name: Discrete-Time First-Order Markov Chain
nodes.statement: An $N$-state stochastic process $\{q_t\}$ satisfying the Markov property $P[q_t = S_j \mid q_{t-1} = S_i, q_{t-2} = S_k, \ldots] = P[q_t = S_j \mid q_{t-1} = S_i]$, with time-homogeneous transitions $a_{ij} = P[q_t = S_j \mid q_{t-1} = S_i]$, $a_{ij} \geq 0$, $\sum_j a_{ij} = 1$.
nodes.statement_clean: Memoryless first-order Markov chain on N states with stationary transition probabilities forming a stochastic matrix.

nodes.name: Hidden Markov Model (HMM)
nodes.statement: A doubly embedded stochastic process whose underlying state sequence is not directly observable but is revealed only through another set of stochastic processes that produce the sequence of observations.
nodes.statement_clean: A Markov chain whose states are hidden and only observed through state-dependent emission distributions.

nodes.name: HMM Parameter Set $\lambda = (A, B, \pi)$
nodes.statement: An HMM is fully specified by: (i) $N$ hidden states $S = \{S_1,\ldots,S_N\}$; (ii) $M$ observation symbols $V = \{v_1,\ldots,v_M\}$; (iii) state-transition matrix $A = \{a_{ij}\}$ with $a_{ij} = P[q_{t+1} = S_j \mid q_t = S_i]$; (iv) emission distribution $B = \{b_j(k)\}$ with $b_j(k) = P[v_k \text{ at } t \mid q_t = S_j]$; (v) initial distribution $\pi = \{\pi_i\}$ with $\pi_i = P[q_1 = S_i]$. Compactly $\lambda = (A, B, \pi)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Five-tuple specifying number of states, alphabet size, transition matrix, emission matrix, and initial distribution.

nodes.name: Forward Variable $\alpha_t(i)$
nodes.statement: $\alpha_t(i) = P(O_1 O_2 \cdots O_t, q_t = S_i \mid \lambda)$, the joint probability of the partial observation sequence up to time $t$ and being in state $S_i$ at time $t$, given the model.
nodes.statement_clean: Probability of observing the prefix and ending in a particular state.

nodes.name: Backward Variable $\beta_t(i)$
nodes.statement: $\beta_t(i) = P(O_{t+1} O_{t+2} \cdots O_T \mid q_t = S_i, \lambda)$, the probability of the partial observation sequence from $t+1$ to the end given state $S_i$ at time $t$ and the model.
nodes.statement_clean: Probability of the remaining observation suffix given a particular current state.

nodes.name: State Posterior $\gamma_t(i)$
nodes.statement: $\gamma_t(i) = P(q_t = S_i \mid O, \lambda) = \dfrac{\alpha_t(i)\beta_t(i)}{\sum_{j=1}^N \alpha_t(j)\beta_t(j)}$, the posterior probability of being in state $S_i$ at time $t$ given the observations and model.
nodes.statement_clean: Per-time-step posterior over hidden states.

nodes.name: Two-State Transition Posterior $\xi_t(i,j)$
nodes.statement: $\xi_t(i,j) = P(q_t = S_i, q_{t+1} = S_j \mid O, \lambda) = \dfrac{\alpha_t(i) a_{ij} b_j(O_{t+1}) \beta_{t+1}(j)}{\sum_{i,j} \alpha_t(i) a_{ij} b_j(O_{t+1}) \beta_{t+1}(j)}$.
nodes.statement_clean: Posterior probability of transitioning from state i to state j between consecutive times.

nodes.name: Viterbi Score $\delta_t(i)$
nodes.statement: $\delta_t(i) = \max_{q_1,\ldots,q_{t-1}} P[q_1 q_2 \cdots q_t = i, O_1 \cdots O_t \mid \lambda]$, the highest joint probability along a single path that accounts for the first $t$ observations and ends in state $S_i$.
nodes.statement_clean: Best-path score ending in a given state at time t.

nodes.name: Ergodic (Fully Connected) HMM
nodes.statement: An HMM in which every state can be reached from every other state in a single step, equivalently $a_{ij} > 0$ for all $i, j$.
nodes.statement_clean: HMM with strictly positive transition matrix.

nodes.name: Left-Right (Bakis) HMM
nodes.statement: An HMM whose state index is non-decreasing along the state sequence, enforced by $a_{ij} = 0$ for $j < i$ (and often $a_{ij} = 0$ for $j > i + \Delta$), with $\pi_i = 1$ for $i = 1$ and $\pi_i = 0$ otherwise.
nodes.statement_clean: HMM whose states proceed from left to right, suitable for time-evolving signals like speech.

nodes.name: Continuous-Density HMM with Gaussian Mixture Emissions
nodes.statement: An HMM whose emission density in state $j$ is a finite mixture $b_j(O) = \sum_{m=1}^M c_{jm} \mathcal{N}(O, \mu_{jm}, U_{jm})$ with $\sum_m c_{jm} = 1$, $c_{jm} \geq 0$.
nodes.statement_clean: HMM with continuous observation vectors modeled by per-state Gaussian mixtures.

nodes.name: Autoregressive HMM
nodes.statement: An HMM whose observation vectors $O$ of length $K$ are drawn from a Gaussian autoregressive process of order $p$, $O_k = -\sum_{i=1}^p a_i O_{k-i} + e_k$, $e_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ i.i.d., with state-conditioned AR coefficients.
nodes.statement_clean: HMM whose state-conditioned emissions are Gaussian AR processes; useful for speech.

nodes.name: Variable-Duration (Explicit-Duration) HMM
nodes.statement: An HMM in which self-transitions are removed and each state $S_i$ carries an explicit state-duration density $p_i(d)$ for the number of consecutive observations emitted before the next state transition.
nodes.statement_clean: HMM that explicitly models how long the chain stays in each state, replacing the implicit geometric self-loop duration.

nodes.name: Null Transition
nodes.statement: A transition between HMM states that produces no observation, denoted by $\phi$; useful for skipping states or representing alternate pronunciations and grammar arcs.
nodes.statement_clean: An emission-free transition allowing state jumps without consuming an observation.

nodes.name: Parameter Tying
nodes.statement: An equivalence relation imposed across HMM parameters in different states (typically $b_j$ densities), reducing the number of free parameters by sharing estimates among tied entries.
nodes.statement_clean: Sharing parameter estimates across multiple states or models to reduce parameter count.

nodes.name: Model Distance $D(\lambda_1, \lambda_2)$
nodes.statement: $D(\lambda_1, \lambda_2) = \frac{1}{T}\bigl[\log P(O^{(2)} \mid \lambda_1) - \log P(O^{(2)} \mid \lambda_2)\bigr]$ where $O^{(2)}$ is generated by $\lambda_2$. The symmetrized version is $D_s(\lambda_1, \lambda_2) = (D(\lambda_1,\lambda_2) + D(\lambda_2,\lambda_1))/2$.
nodes.statement_clean: A log-likelihood-ratio dissimilarity measure between two HMMs.

nodes.name: Vector Quantization (VQ) Codebook
nodes.statement: A partition of the observation vector space into $M$ disjoint cells, each represented by a centroid $v_m$, designed iteratively to minimize average spectral distortion; observations are mapped to the index of the nearest centroid.
nodes.statement_clean: Discretization of continuous feature vectors via nearest-centroid coding.

nodes.name: Problem 1 — Evaluation
nodes.statement: Given an observation sequence $O = O_1 O_2 \cdots O_T$ and a model $\lambda = (A, B, \pi)$, efficiently compute $P(O \mid \lambda)$, the probability of the observations given the model.
nodes.statement_clean: Compute the likelihood of an observation sequence under an HMM.

nodes.name: Problem 2 — Decoding (Best State Sequence)
nodes.statement: Given $O$ and $\lambda$, choose a state sequence $Q = q_1 q_2 \cdots q_T$ that is optimal in some meaningful sense (e.g., maximizes $P(Q \mid O, \lambda)$).
nodes.statement_clean: Recover the most likely hidden state sequence given observations.

nodes.name: Problem 3 — Parameter Estimation (Training)
nodes.statement: Adjust the model parameters $\lambda = (A, B, \pi)$ to maximize $P(O \mid \lambda)$ for an observed training sequence.
nodes.statement_clean: Train HMM parameters from data by maximum likelihood.

nodes.name: Isolated Word Recognition
nodes.statement: Given a vocabulary of $V$ words, each modeled by a distinct HMM $\lambda^v$, and an observation sequence $O$ for an unknown spoken word, choose $v^* = \arg\max_{1 \leq v \leq V} P(O \mid \lambda^v)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Classify an isolated spoken word among V candidate HMM word models by maximum likelihood.

nodes.name: Connected Word Recognition
nodes.statement: Given an observation sequence representing a continuous utterance composed of words from a vocabulary, find the optimum sequence of word HMMs (their concatenation) that best matches $O$ in the maximum-likelihood sense.
nodes.statement_clean: Recognize a string of concatenated spoken words by jointly segmenting and identifying them.

nodes.name: Forward Algorithm
nodes.statement: Inductive procedure that computes $\alpha_t(i)$ on a trellis in $O(N^2 T)$ operations and returns $P(O \mid \lambda) = \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_T(i)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Trellis-based forward recursion solving Problem 1 efficiently.

nodes.name: Backward Algorithm
nodes.statement: Inductive backward recursion that computes $\beta_t(i)$ on the trellis in $O(N^2 T)$ operations.
nodes.statement_clean: Backward counterpart of the forward algorithm; needed for posterior computations and Baum-Welch.

nodes.name: Viterbi Algorithm
nodes.statement: Dynamic-programming procedure that computes the single best state sequence $q^* = \arg\max_Q P(Q, O \mid \lambda)$ along with $P^* = \max_Q P(Q, O \mid \lambda)$ via $\delta_t(j) = \max_i [\delta_{t-1}(i) a_{ij}] b_j(O_t)$ and backtracking through stored argmax pointers $\psi_t(j)$.
nodes.statement_clean: DP algorithm solving Problem 2 (most likely state path).

nodes.name: Baum-Welch (Forward-Backward) Reestimation
nodes.statement: Iterative EM-style procedure that, given current $\lambda$, computes $\bar\pi_i = \gamma_1(i)$, $\bar a_{ij} = \sum_t \xi_t(i,j) / \sum_t \gamma_t(i)$, and $\bar b_j(k) = \sum_{t: O_t = v_k} \gamma_t(j) / \sum_t \gamma_t(j)$, monotonically improving $P(O \mid \lambda)$ until a critical point.
nodes.statement_clean: Iterative reestimation that locally maximizes the observation likelihood by reassigning expected counts.
output: Reestimated HMM $\bar\lambda = (\bar A, \bar B, \bar\pi)$ with $P(O \mid \bar\lambda) \geq P(O \mid \lambda)$

nodes.name: Scaled Forward-Backward Procedure
nodes.statement: Modification of the forward-backward computation that, at each time $t$, scales $\alpha_t(i)$ by $c_t = 1/\sum_i \alpha_t(i)$ and applies the same scale factors to $\beta_t(i)$, preventing underflow without affecting reestimation; the log-likelihood is recovered via $\log P(O\mid\lambda) = -\sum_t \log c_t$.
nodes.statement_clean: Numerically stable rescaling of forward-backward to handle long sequences.

nodes.name: Multiple-Sequence Reestimation
nodes.statement: Modified Baum-Welch for $K$ independent observation sequences $O = [O^{(1)}, \ldots, O^{(K)}]$ that maximizes $\prod_k P(O^{(k)} \mid \lambda)$ by summing per-sequence frequency contributions divided by per-sequence likelihoods $P_k$.
nodes.statement_clean: Pooled training over multiple independent observation sequences (essential for left-right HMMs).
output: Reestimated $\bar\lambda$ maximizing joint likelihood across sequences

nodes.name: Variable-Duration HMM Reestimation
nodes.statement: Forward-backward reestimation extended with starred forward/backward variables ($\alpha_t^*, \beta_t^*$) that incorporate the explicit state-duration density $p_i(d)$ truncated at maximum duration $D$; reestimates $a_{ij}$, $b_j(k)$, and $p_i(d)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Extended Baum-Welch handling explicit per-state duration densities.

nodes.name: Deleted Interpolation
nodes.statement: Procedure that combats sparse data by interpolating two model parameter sets $\bar\lambda = \epsilon\lambda + (1-\epsilon)\lambda'$ where $\lambda'$ is a reduced (well-trained) model and $\epsilon$ is estimated by a forward-backward procedure on a held-out partition of the training data.
nodes.statement_clean: Mix a richer model with a reduced model to compensate for limited training data.

nodes.name: Segmental K-Means Training
nodes.statement: Training procedure that alternates Viterbi state segmentation of the observation sequences with K-means clustering of within-state observations to update emission parameters, looping until model convergence by a distance criterion.
nodes.statement_clean: Faster initialization/training that segments via Viterbi and clusters via K-means in each loop.
output: Reestimated HMM parameters (mixture weights $c_{jm}$, means $\hat\mu_{jm}$, covariances $\hat U_{jm}$, transitions $a_{ij}$)

nodes.name: Level-Building Connected-Word Recognizer
nodes.statement: Three-stage connected-word recognizer that (1) extracts spectral features, (2) performs Viterbi level-building pattern matching of single-word HMMs across levels $\ell = 1, \ldots, L$ to produce candidate digit strings, and (3) postprocesses to enforce duration constraints and select the best candidate.
nodes.statement_clean: Connected-word HMM recognizer using Viterbi-based level-building pattern matching with a post-processor.
nodes.origin_citation: Rabiner, Wilpon, Juang 1986; Rabiner, Wilpon, Levinson 1985

nodes.name: Baum-Welch Likelihood Increase
nodes.statement: If $\lambda$ is not at a critical point of the likelihood and $\bar\lambda$ is the reestimate produced by the Baum-Welch update, then $P(O \mid \bar\lambda) > P(O \mid \lambda)$; iterating yields a sequence whose likelihood converges to a critical point of $P(O \mid \lambda)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Baum-Welch reestimation never decreases the observation likelihood and converges to a local maximum.
nodes.origin_citation: Baum, Petrie, Soules, Weiss 1970; Baum & Sell 1968

nodes.name: Auxiliary-Function Maximization Implies Likelihood Increase
nodes.statement: Define $Q(\lambda, \bar\lambda) = \sum_Q P(Q, O \mid \lambda) \log P(Q, O \mid \bar\lambda)$. Then $\max_{\bar\lambda} Q(\lambda, \bar\lambda) \Rightarrow P(O \mid \bar\lambda) \geq P(O \mid \lambda)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Maximizing Baum's auxiliary Q-function in the modification step never decreases the observation likelihood.

nodes.name: Equivalence of Baum-Welch and EM
nodes.statement: The Baum-Welch reestimation formulas (40a)-(40c) are exactly the E and M steps of the Expectation-Maximization algorithm applied to the HMM likelihood: the E-step computes $Q(\lambda, \bar\lambda)$ and the M-step maximizes it over $\bar\lambda$.
nodes.statement_clean: Baum-Welch is a special case of EM for the HMM model.
conclusions: Baum-Welch updates equal the EM updates for the HMM likelihood

nodes.name: Lagrange Critical-Point Form of Reestimation
nodes.statement: Subject to the stochastic constraints $\sum_i \bar\pi_i = 1$, $\sum_j \bar a_{ij} = 1$, $\sum_k \bar b_j(k) = 1$, the maximum of $P = P(O \mid \lambda)$ satisfies $\pi_i = \dfrac{\pi_i \partial P/\partial \pi_i}{\sum_k \pi_k \partial P/\partial \pi_k}$, $a_{ij} = \dfrac{a_{ij} \partial P/\partial a_{ij}}{\sum_k a_{ik} \partial P/\partial a_{ik}}$, $b_j(k) = \dfrac{b_j(k) \partial P/\partial b_j(k)}{\sum_\ell b_j(\ell) \partial P/\partial b_j(\ell)}$. The Baum-Welch reestimates are precisely fixed points of these equations.
nodes.statement_clean: Stochastic-constrained Lagrange optimality conditions for HMM parameters reduce to the Baum-Welch fixed-point form.
conclusions: Fixed-point equations (44a)-(44c) characterize critical points of $P(O \mid \lambda)$

nodes.name: Geometric State-Duration Density
nodes.statement: For a standard HMM, the probability of remaining in state $S_i$ for exactly $d$ consecutive observations is $p_i(d) = (a_{ii})^{d-1}(1 - a_{ii})$, with expected duration $\bar d_i = 1/(1 - a_{ii})$.
nodes.statement_clean: Self-transition probabilities induce a geometric duration distribution on each state.

nodes.name: Ergodic Equivalence of Distinct HMMs
nodes.statement: Two two-state HMMs $\lambda_1 = (A_1, B_1, \pi_1)$ and $\lambda_2 = (A_2, B_2, \pi_2)$ with $\pi_1 = \pi_2 = [1/2, 1/2]$, $A_i$ and $B_i$ given by symmetric stochastic forms parameterized by $p, q$ (resp. $r, s$), have $E[O_t \mid \lambda_1] = E[O_t \mid \lambda_2]$ iff $pq + (1-p)(1-q) = rs + (1-r)(1-s)$, equivalently $s = (p + q - 2pq)/(1 - 2r)$. Hence statistically equivalent HMMs need not have equal $A$ and $B$.
nodes.statement_clean: Two HMMs can produce identical observation marginals while having quite different transition and emission matrices.
assumptions: Two two-state HMMs with the symmetric form above
conclusions: Equality of expected symbol probabilities reduces to a quadratic relation; distinct $(A, B)$ can satisfy it

nodes.name: Forward Recursion
nodes.statement: $\alpha_1(i) = \pi_i b_i(O_1)$, $\alpha_{t+1}(j) = \bigl[\sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_t(i) a_{ij}\bigr] b_j(O_{t+1})$, with termination $P(O \mid \lambda) = \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_T(i)$.

nodes.name: Backward Recursion
nodes.statement: $\beta_T(i) = 1$, $\beta_t(i) = \sum_{j=1}^N a_{ij} b_j(O_{t+1}) \beta_{t+1}(j)$.

nodes.name: Viterbi Recursion
nodes.statement: $\delta_1(i) = \pi_i b_i(O_1)$, $\delta_t(j) = \max_i [\delta_{t-1}(i) a_{ij}] b_j(O_t)$, $\psi_t(j) = \arg\max_i [\delta_{t-1}(i) a_{ij}]$, with termination $P^* = \max_i \delta_T(i)$, $q_T^* = \arg\max_i \delta_T(i)$, and backtracking $q_t^* = \psi_{t+1}(q_{t+1}^*)$.

nodes.name: Baum-Welch Reestimation Formulas
nodes.statement: $\bar\pi_i = \gamma_1(i)$; $\bar a_{ij} = \sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \xi_t(i,j) / \sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \gamma_t(i)$; $\bar b_j(k) = \sum_{t: O_t = v_k} \gamma_t(j) / \sum_{t=1}^T \gamma_t(j)$.

nodes.name: Continuous Mixture Reestimation
nodes.statement: $\bar c_{jk} = \dfrac{\sum_t \gamma_t(j,k)}{\sum_t \sum_m \gamma_t(j,m)}$, $\bar\mu_{jk} = \dfrac{\sum_t \gamma_t(j,k) O_t}{\sum_t \gamma_t(j,k)}$, $\bar U_{jk} = \dfrac{\sum_t \gamma_t(j,k)(O_t - \mu_{jk})(O_t - \mu_{jk})'}{\sum_t \gamma_t(j,k)}$, with $\gamma_t(j,k)$ the posterior probability of state $j$ and mixture component $k$ at time $t$.

nodes.name: Log-Likelihood from Scale Factors
nodes.statement: $\prod_{t=1}^T c_t \cdot P(O \mid \lambda) = 1$, hence $\log P(O \mid \lambda) = -\sum_{t=1}^T \log c_t$.

nodes.name: Markov and Output-Independence Assumptions
nodes.statement: (i) The hidden state sequence is a first-order Markov chain: $P[q_t \mid q_{t-1}, q_{t-2}, \ldots] = P[q_t \mid q_{t-1}]$. (ii) Successive observations are conditionally independent given the state sequence: $P(O_1, \ldots, O_T \mid Q, \lambda) = \prod_t P(O_t \mid q_t, \lambda)$.
nodes.statement_clean: HMM relies on first-order state Markovity and conditional output independence given the state.

nodes.name: Three-State Weather Markov Model
nodes.statement: Three-state observable Markov chain (rain, cloudy, sunny) with transition matrix $A$ given in (3); given $q_1 = $ sunny, the probability of the sequence sun-sun-rain-rain-sun-cloudy-sun is computed as $\pi_3 a_{33}^2 a_{31} a_{11} a_{13} a_{32} a_{23} \approx 1.536 \times 10^{-4}$.
nodes.statement_clean: Worked example of evaluating a path probability in an observable 3-state weather Markov chain.

nodes.name: Coin-Toss HMMs (1-, 2-, 3-coin Models)
nodes.statement: Three candidate HMMs explaining a hidden coin-tossing experiment: (a) 1-coin (1 unknown parameter), (b) 2-coin (4 unknowns), (c) 3-coin (9 unknowns), illustrating the trade-off between model expressiveness and identifiability.
nodes.statement_clean: Pedagogical example contrasting HMMs with 1, 2, or 3 hidden coins for the same observation sequence.

nodes.name: Urn-and-Ball Model
nodes.statement: $N$-state HMM in which each state is an urn containing colored balls in known proportions; a hidden 'genie' selects an urn (state transition) and draws a ball (observation), yielding a discrete-symbol HMM with state-dependent emission distributions.
nodes.statement_clean: Classic urn-and-ball metaphor for a discrete-symbol HMM.

nodes.name: Three Topologies of HMMs (4-state ergodic, 4-state left-right, 6-state parallel-path)
nodes.statement: Fig. 7 illustrates a 4-state ergodic HMM, a 4-state left-right (Bakis) HMM with $\Delta = 2$, and a 6-state parallel-path left-right HMM, contrasting the structural form of the transition matrix in each case.
nodes.statement_clean: Three representative HMM topologies used in practice.

nodes.name: Isolated-Digit Recognition Experiment
nodes.statement: Speaker-independent recognition of isolated English digits with 100 talkers training and 100 talkers in test sets TS2-TS4; digit error rates compared across LPC/DTW, LPC/DTW/VQ, HMM/VQ, HMM/CD (continuous density, $M=5$), and HMM/AR recognizers (Table 1).
nodes.statement_clean: Comparative isolated-digit recognition experiment showing HMM/CD comparable to template-based DTW and superior to HMM/AR.

nodes.name: Connected-Digit Recognition Experiment
nodes.statement: Three modes of HMM connected-digit recognition (speaker-trained, multispeaker, speaker-independent on TI database) evaluated under unknown- and known-length scoring; reported string error rates in Table 2 (e.g., 1.65% KL on the TI test set).
nodes.statement_clean: Connected-digit recognition experiments demonstrating HMM-based recognizer performance across speaker conditions.

nodes.name: 5-State Word Model with Empirical Duration Densities for 'six'
nodes.statement: 5-state left-right word HMM for the digit 'six' whose per-state normalized duration densities $p_i(d/T)$ (Fig. 20) align with the phonetic structure: states 1-2 capture /s/, state 3 the transition, state 4 the vowel /i/, and state 5 the final stop and /s/.
nodes.statement_clean: Empirical state-duration densities for the digit 'six' show phonetically meaningful state assignments.

nodes.name: Three Fundamental HMM Problems Frame the Theory
nodes.statement: All practical HMM use rests on solving Problems 1, 2, and 3: evaluation, decoding, and parameter estimation; the rest of the paper develops algorithmic solutions to each and applies them to speech recognition tasks.

nodes.name: Direct Likelihood Computation Is Intractable
nodes.statement: Direct evaluation of $P(O \mid \lambda) = \sum_Q P(O \mid Q, \lambda) P(Q \mid \lambda)$ requires on the order of $2T \cdot N^T$ operations (e.g., $\sim 10^{72}$ for $N = 5$, $T = 100$), motivating the trellis-based forward-backward procedure with $O(N^2 T)$ cost.

nodes.name: Limitations of HMMs
nodes.statement: Conventional HMMs assume conditional output independence, that emission densities are well represented by Gaussian/AR mixtures, and the first-order Markov property — assumptions that are inappropriate for many speech sounds whose dependencies extend across multiple frames.

nodes.name: Local-Maxima Caveat for Baum-Welch
nodes.statement: The forward-backward algorithm yields only a local maximum of the likelihood; the optimization surface for HMMs is highly non-convex, so good initial parameter estimates are essential, especially for continuous emission densities.

nodes.name: MMI and MDI Alternatives to Maximum Likelihood
nodes.statement: Two alternatives to ML training for HMMs are Maximum Mutual Information (MMI), which maximizes the mutual information between the observation sequence and the complete model set $\lambda = (\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_V)$, and Minimum Discrimination Information (MDI), which minimizes a cross-entropy criterion using the generalized Baum algorithm.
nodes.origin_citation: Bahl, Brown, de Souza, Mercer 1986; Ephraim, Dembo, Rabiner 1987

nodes.name: Proof Sketch of Baum-Welch Likelihood Increase
nodes.statement: Apply Baum's auxiliary-function inequality (TP375.2): the reestimation step maximizes $Q(\lambda, \bar\lambda)$ over $\bar\lambda$ subject to the stochastic constraints, and Baum's lemma then gives $P(O \mid \bar\lambda) \geq P(O \mid \lambda)$, with strict inequality unless $\lambda$ is a critical point. Iteration produces a monotone-increasing bounded sequence converging to a critical point.

nodes.name: Apply auxiliary-function inequality
nodes.statement: Invoke Baum's lemma: $\max_{\bar\lambda} Q(\lambda, \bar\lambda) \Rightarrow P(O \mid \bar\lambda) \geq P(O \mid \lambda)$ (TP375.2).

nodes.name: Identify reestimates as constrained Q-maximizers
nodes.statement: Show via Lagrange multipliers (PrP375.2) that the Baum-Welch updates $\bar\pi, \bar a_{ij}, \bar b_j(k)$ are precisely the maximizers of $Q(\lambda, \bar\lambda)$ subject to the stochastic constraints (43a)-(43c).

nodes.name: Conclude monotone convergence
nodes.statement: Combining PSP375.1 and PSP375.2 yields $P(O \mid \bar\lambda) \geq P(O \mid \lambda)$ each iteration; since $P(O \mid \lambda) \leq 1$, the iterates converge to a critical point.

nodes.name: Initialization
nodes.statement: $\alpha_1(i) = \pi_i b_i(O_1)$ for $1 \leq i \leq N$.

nodes.name: Induction
nodes.statement: For $t = 1, \ldots, T-1$ and $1 \leq j \leq N$: $\alpha_{t+1}(j) = \bigl[\sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_t(i) a_{ij}\bigr] b_j(O_{t+1})$.

nodes.name: Termination
nodes.statement: $P(O \mid \lambda) = \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_T(i)$.

nodes.name: Initialization of Viterbi DP
nodes.statement: $\delta_1(i) = \pi_i b_i(O_1)$, $\psi_1(i) = 0$ for $1 \leq i \leq N$.

nodes.name: Recursion with argmax pointers
nodes.statement: For $2 \leq t \leq T$, $1 \leq j \leq N$: $\delta_t(j) = \max_i [\delta_{t-1}(i) a_{ij}] b_j(O_t)$ and $\psi_t(j) = \arg\max_i [\delta_{t-1}(i) a_{ij}]$.

nodes.name: Termination
nodes.statement: $P^* = \max_i \delta_T(i)$, $q_T^* = \arg\max_i \delta_T(i)$.

nodes.name: Backtracking
nodes.statement: For $t = T-1, T-2, \ldots, 1$: $q_t^* = \psi_{t+1}(q_{t+1}^*)$. Return state sequence $q_1^* \cdots q_T^*$.

nodes.name: E-step: forward-backward
nodes.statement: Run the forward (AP375.1) and backward (AP375.2) algorithms to obtain $\alpha_t(i)$ and $\beta_t(i)$; compute $\gamma_t(i)$ and $\xi_t(i,j)$.

nodes.name: M-step: reestimate $(\bar\pi, \bar A, \bar B)$
nodes.statement: Set $\bar\pi_i = \gamma_1(i)$, $\bar a_{ij} = \sum_t \xi_t(i,j) / \sum_t \gamma_t(i)$, $\bar b_j(k) = \sum_{t: O_t = v_k} \gamma_t(j) / \sum_t \gamma_t(j)$.

nodes.name: Iterate to convergence
nodes.statement: Replace $\lambda \leftarrow \bar\lambda$ and repeat the E and M steps until $P(O \mid \lambda)$ stops increasing or a tolerance is reached.

nodes.name: Model initialization
nodes.statement: Choose initial HMM $\lambda$ (random, uniform segmentation, or borrowed from prior model).

nodes.name: Viterbi state segmentation
nodes.statement: Run Viterbi (AP375.3) on each training sequence under current $\lambda$ to assign each observation to a state.

nodes.name: K-means clustering within states
nodes.statement: For each state $j$, cluster the within-state observation vectors into $M$ clusters by Euclidean K-means and update $\hat c_{jm}, \hat\mu_{jm}, \hat U_{jm}$ from the resulting partitions; update $a_{ij}$ from segmentation transition counts.

nodes.name: Convergence test and reestimation loop
nodes.statement: Compute model distance to previous $\lambda$; if above threshold, replace $\lambda$ with the new model and repeat from segmentation, else exit and run final formal Baum-Welch reestimation if desired.
